newsitem.title: USA: Exide to close four European battery plants.
newsitem.headline: Exide to close four European battery plants.

text.p: Exide Corp said it plans to close four battery making plants in Europe in its 1998 fiscal year which began April 1, but the financial health of the company looks set to improve futher.

"Our outlook for financial performance for fiscal 1998 is truly outstanding," Exide's Chairman, President and CEO Arthur Hawkins told an analyst conference call on Wednesday, later made available on tape.

Profits in North America will be boosted following a decision by Sears, Roebuck and Co to expand over three years Exide's role as a supplier of batteries to the company, thereby increasing its North American market share, Hawkins said.
The company's new NASCAR battery and battery accessories will also generate extra profits, Hawkins added.
Exide is the world's biggest producer of batteries and a key player in the lead market.
Exide announced Tuesday a loss of 37 cents per share in the fourth quarter of its 1997 fiscal year. Net income for fiscal 1997 was 90 cents per share.
A mild winter in North America forced Exide to cut battery production by a million units in the fourth quarter.
Restructuring and closing some European plants in fiscal 1997 along with non-recurring changes in balance sheet reporting also dented results. Some 1,000 staff at Exide were laid off in fiscal 1997.
Sales in North America were already up 11 percent in April and May compared to the same two months in 1997, Hawkins said. Sales in Europe in April were flat to off 2 percent.
Four battery making plants in Europe will be closed in fiscal 1998, Dagenham in the U.K., Nimes and Vierzon in France, and Horten in Norway, giving rise to $24 million in benefits, Hawkins said.
And a further two plants will close in Germany following the takeover of CEAG AG or Data, with the loss of some 500 jobs, Hawkins said.
Some two-thirds of Exide's business in now in Europe following a string of acquisitions in recent year. The takeover of Data in Germany is set to be concluded mid-July, Exide officials said.
Hawkins said Exide had performed well in Europe compared to several rivals such as VARTA and others who faced financial difficulties or made losses.
Hawkins said Exide still intended to supply itself half of the lead needed by its European plants by the end of the century.
Exide said it was now buying lead on a monthly basis in Europe after buying forward for the year in fiscal 1997 at significantly above the market.
"We will continue to buying on a monthly basis until we can figure out which way the market is going. None of our people can get a handle on it," Hawkins said.
In the U.S., Exide is integrated with its own lead supplies.
